explanations.answer: Runs ahead and climbs a tree
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Luke 19:4 says he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus, since Jesus was about to pass that way. He figured out where Jesus was headed and got there first. A man with a plan and a branch.

explanations.answer: Pushes his way to the front
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say he shoved anybody. Luke 19:4 says he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree. I think a crowd that thick is hard to shove through anyway. Zacchaeus went over it instead of through it.

explanations.answer: Asks the crowd to let him through
explanations.explanation: Nice and polite, but that's not what happened. The text says he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him (Luke 19:4). I'd have asked too, honestly, and then I'd have been squished in the back like a cookie at the bottom of the box. Zacchaeus went up instead.

explanations.answer: He must stay at his house today
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Jesus says, “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.” (Luke 19:5) Nobody invited Jesus. He did the inviting. And He picked the man up in the tree.

explanations.answer: The crowd is about to block the road
explanations.explanation: The crowd is there, but Jesus never mentions it. His reason is, “…for I must stay at your house today.” (Luke 19:5) The text gives the reason, so I'll stick with it. It's about a visit.

explanations.answer: He has a message for all of Jericho
explanations.explanation: Jesus is passing through Jericho, but this moment is about one house. He says, “…for I must stay at your house today.” (Luke 19:5) Your house, singular. I think Zacchaeus heard that and nearly fell out of the tree.
Joyfully is it, baker. Luke 19:6 says Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. He didn't take the slow way down either. He hurried.
I might have been nervous myself, but the text doesn't say that. Luke 19:6 says he hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. Hurrying and joy. That's the whole description.

Quiet would've been my guess for a man caught up a tree. But Luke 19:6 says he hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. Joy doesn't sound like a whisper to me, but I'll let the text have the last word.

explanations.answer: He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. All who saw it began to grumble, saying, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (Luke 19:7) Everybody had a comment and nobody had been asked. Grumbling travels fast.

explanations.answer: He has gone to be the guest of a Pharisee
explanations.explanation: Different crowd, different complaint. The grumblers said, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (Luke 19:7) The text doesn't mention a Pharisee in this scene. The complaint was about Zacchaeus.

explanations.answer: He has passed by the rest of Jericho
explanations.explanation: That's a creative one, baker. But the people said, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (Luke 19:7) Their complaint was about who Jesus was staying with. They were grumbling, and they said it out loud.

Half is right, baker. Zacchaeus says, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor…” (Luke 19:8) A very wealthy man, and half goes out the door. I've given away a cookie before and felt it. This is a whole different level.

A tenth is a number people know well, but it's not the one here. Zacchaeus says, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor…” (Luke 19:8) Half is a lot bigger than a tenth. Big math for a man who was just up a tree.
All would've been something, baker. But Zacchaeus says, “…half of my possessions I give to the poor…” (Luke 19:8) Half. I won't make it bigger than the text does.
Fourfold, baker. Zacchaeus says, “…if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” (Luke 19:8) Four times. I couldn't even return a borrowed rolling pin on time, so this humbles me.

Half is what he says about his possessions and the poor. For cheating, he says, “…if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” (Luke 19:8) Fourfold is way more than half. Good mix-up, since both numbers are in the same verse.
The courts never come up. Zacchaeus says, “…if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” (Luke 19:8) He's the one saying what he will do. It's all in the first person.
Salvation, baker. Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house…” (Luke 19:9) Today, not someday. It came to the house of the man the crowd was grumbling about.
The crowd may have expected something like that, but Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house…” (Luke 19:9) Salvation is the word. The grumblers were wrong about where this was headed.
I can see why you'd think so, since everybody was grumbling. But Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house…” (Luke 19:9) Salvation came, and trouble didn't.

explanations.answer: This man too is a son of Abraham
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…this man too is a son of Abraham.” (Luke 19:9) Abraham is the father of Israel's people, and Jesus says Zacchaeus belongs among them. The crowd had called him a sinful man, and Jesus called him a son of Abraham.

explanations.answer: This man has kept the whole law
explanations.explanation: The text never says that. Jesus gives this reason: “…this man too is a son of Abraham.” (Luke 19:9) Abraham was the father of Israel's people. Jesus doesn't point to a perfect record. He points to who Zacchaeus is.

explanations.answer: This man was first to see Me
explanations.explanation: Zacchaeus did climb a tree to see Jesus, so I get it. But Jesus's reason is, “…this man too is a son of Abraham.” (Luke 19:9) Nothing about being first. If it were a race, I think the tree gave him an edge anyway.

Lost, baker. Jesus says, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” (Luke 19:10) Seek and save. I sat in the back of a drawer for years, so this line gets me every time. Somebody came looking.
I understand why that sounds right, but it isn't the word. Jesus says, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” (Luke 19:10) The word is lost. Zacchaeus just got found, up a tree.

Powerful would fit a man who was wealthy, a chief tax collector with a title. But Jesus says, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” (Luke 19:10) The word is lost. Money and rank didn't change that, and Jesus came for him anyway.
